thesis_statement: Urban community gardens improve neighborhood food security by increasing access to fresh produce and strengthening local food-distribution networks.

body_paragraphs.topic_sentence: Community gardens directly increase access to fresh produce for residents in food deserts.
evidence: A 2019 USDA survey found households within walking distance of a community garden reported 23% higher weekly vegetable consumption.
Case study of the Detroit Garden Resource Program showed participating families reduced grocery spending on produce by an average of $150 per season.
body_paragraphs.link_back_to_thesis: This increased access to fresh produce is a direct mechanism by which community gardens improve neighborhood food security.

body_paragraphs.topic_sentence: Community gardens also strengthen local food-distribution networks by creating informal produce-sharing channels.
evidence: Interviews with garden coordinators in Portland documented surplus-sharing arrangements with three neighboring food pantries.
A 2021 study of 40 community gardens found 68% had a formal or informal surplus-donation agreement with a local organization.
body_paragraphs.link_back_to_thesis: These distribution networks extend the food-security benefit of community gardens beyond the gardeners themselves, reinforcing the thesis.

conclusion.restates_thesis: By increasing access to fresh produce and strengthening local food-distribution networks, community gardens improve neighborhood food security.
